headline: Sea Bright to Manasquan: blues by the dozen, bass by the grace of God
subhead: Dawn patrol on the rocks turned up cocktail blues and short fluke — the slot bass showed up for maybe twenty minutes a day, and you had to be standing in the right spot.
body_markdown:
Quarter to six Tuesday morning, north jetty at Manasquan, and there were four of us out there in the gray light before the sun cleared the roofline of the Coast Guard station. Nobody was talking. That's how you know it's July — everybody's saving their breath for the cast, not the small talk. A guy I've seen out there since Memorial Day was working a black Gibbs pencil popper along the tip, and on maybe his sixth cast the water just erupted. Not a bass blowup — that slow, deliberate porpoise-roll thing stripers do. This was violent, scattershot, half a dozen fish crashing at once. Cocktail blues, two to four pounds, and they stayed on top for a solid twenty minutes before the school moved off toward Shark River. That's been the pattern all week up and down this stretch — the bluefish are the ones showing up to work, and the bass are punching a very short clock.

I won't sugarcoat it. Striped bass fishing on the jetties right now is a dawn-and-dusk proposition, and even then it's thin. The ocean's sitting around 71-72 degrees off the beach — that's warm enough that the quality bass have slid off into deeper, cooler water or pushed north looking for bait, and what's left in close on the rocks are mostly schoolies in the 18-24 inch range, with the occasional slot fish mixed in if you're fishing the right two hours of tide. I had one 29-incher come off the Sea Bright rocks Sunday night on a bunker chunk fished on a fish-finder rig in about 12 feet of water, dead low tide turning to the first push of the flood — that first hour of moving water after a long slack is when something bigger will slide through to feed, and it's usually the only window you get. After that the current builds, the day boats come out, the jet skis show up, and the bite shuts like a door.

Eels are still your best bet for a real fish after dark. I've had guys tell me about 30-inch-class bass coming off the Manasquan Inlet rocks and the Spring Lake jetties on live eels, fished on the last two hours of the outgoing when there's still enough current to make the eel swim natural instead of just hanging there like a dead worm. That's a night program — headlamp, sneakers with the felt soles if you've still got them, and patience, because you might throw for two hours before one fish hits. Nobody's filling a cooler doing this. But if you want a real bass instead of a dink, that's the play right now.

The better news is the fluke. Manasquan and Shark River Inlets have both been giving up decent numbers on the drift — 4-inch white and pink Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, bounced slow along the bottom in 15 to 25 feet on the last of the outgoing when the current's still got some snap to it but isn't ripping your line sideways. Most of what's coming over the rail is short, 14 to 17 inches, but there's a keeper mixed in for every eight or ten fish, and a couple guys working the deeper hole just inside the Manasquan Inlet rock pile have put 3 and 4-pound fluke in the cooler this week on strip baits — squid and fluke belly combos — fished tight to bottom on the last hour before the tide goes dead.

Porgies have been thick on the jetty structure at high water — Belmar and the Spring Lake rocks especially — and if you're tired of getting skunked on bass, a bucket of clams and a high-low rig with size 4 or 6 hooks will keep a rod bending for as long as you want to stand there. Not glamorous, but it's honest fishing and the kids on the rocks with me Tuesday morning went home with a mess of them for the pan.

No albies yet — it's mid-July, too early, don't let anybody tell you different. That pattern doesn't usually light up around here until the back half of September when the bait starts pushing out of the back bays and the water starts dropping through the mid-60s. Blackfish are out of season through the summer months on most of this stretch, so leave the crab pots at home for now.

Looking ahead, the wave state offshore has been rough — 3-plus feet at a short period, which means dirty water and a harder push against the jetty faces, and that's been part of what's kept the bigger bass from committing close to the rocks during daylight. If the wind lays down over the weekend like it's supposed to and the swell drops, I'd expect the water to clean up enough that the dawn bite on top — poppers and darters worked along current seams at first light — gets a little more consistent. The moon's building toward the next new phase, which should push some extra water through the inlets on the exchange tides; that's usually good for stirring the bait and getting stripers to commit for that short window before the sun gets high. If I had one morning to fish this week, I'd be on the Manasquan north jetty an hour before official sunrise, throwing a pencil popper on the last of the ebb, and I'd have a bucktail rigged as backup the second the blues show up instead.
